title: Ledger
description: A double-entry accounting library with no opinions about your database.
imageAlt: Printed ledger sheets and a brass ruler on paper
content:
Ledger is a small library for double-entry bookkeeping. It does one thing: it holds a set of accounts and refuses to let them fall out of balance. It has no schema, no migrations, and no idea what a customer is.

I wrote it after the third time I watched a team reinvent accounting inside an invoicing feature, badly, with a single balance column that four different code paths were allowed to write to.

The design

Everything is an entry, entries come in transactions, and a transaction that does not sum to zero is rejected before it is stored. That single invariant removes an entire category of bug — the one where a refund succeeds, a ledger write fails, and nobody notices for six weeks.

  • No persistence layer — you hand it a repository interface and it does not care what is behind it
  • Balances are derived, never stored, with an optional checkpoint if you have millions of rows
  • Currency is a value object, and mixing two of them is a type error rather than a rounding error

What I learned

The hard part was not the arithmetic. It was resisting every request to add a feature that would have made the library know about invoices. Each one was reasonable in isolation, and each one would have made it useless for the next person.

It is used in production by four companies I know of and an unknown number I do not, which is exactly the right amount of contact to have with a library you maintain in the evenings.

title: Halftone
description: A shader playground for turning photographs into printed matter in the browser.
imageAlt: Macro study of an overlapping halftone dot pattern
content:
Halftone started as a question: how close can a browser get to the look of a photograph printed on newsprint, in real time, without a single image round-trip?

Closer than I expected. The answer is a fragment shader, a rotated dot grid per channel, and a great deal of fiddling with the angle between the screens to avoid moiré.

The interesting part

Print halftones rotate each ink's dot grid to a different angle — traditionally fifteen, seventy-five, zero, and forty-five degrees — precisely so that the patterns do not interfere. Reproduce those angles and the result reads as printed. Get them wrong by three degrees and you get a rosette pattern crawling across the image, which is either a bug or the entire point, depending on the afternoon.

Every reproduction technology has a signature. The signature is what makes it feel like a thing rather than a picture of a thing.

Where it went

It became a tool I use constantly for making textures, and a demo I use to explain to designers why the GPU is not scary. The whole thing is about two hundred lines, most of which are the controls.

title: Casefile
description: Research notes for interview-heavy teams, built around the transcript rather than the tag.
imageAlt: Index cards and interview transcripts fanned out on paper
content:
Casefile is a tool for teams who run a lot of user interviews and lose most of what they learn. I built the first version in six weeks with two researchers sitting next to me, which is the only reason it is any good.

The wrong model

Every research tool I looked at was built around tags. You transcribe an interview, you highlight passages, you tag them, and later you filter by tag. It is a sound model that fails for one reason: tagging is work you do now for a benefit you get later, and under deadline pressure nobody does it.

So Casefile inverts it. The transcript is the primary object, search is full-text and instant, and tags are something you apply while reading the results rather than before. The work happens at the moment you have a question, which is the moment you are actually motivated.

What made it click

  • Quotes carry their surrounding thirty seconds, so a pasted quote can never lose its context
  • Every quote knows which participant said it and links back to the moment in the recording
  • A synthesis is a document that references quotes live — edit the quote, the synthesis updates

That last one was the feature researchers described as the reason they stopped using a spreadsheet.

title: Northlight
description: A design system for a clinical product, where getting a colour wrong is a safety issue.
imageAlt: A printed design-system specimen sheet with swatches and rules
content:
Northlight is the design system behind a clinical documentation product used in hospital wards. The constraints were unlike anything I had worked with, and they made almost every decision for me.

The constraints

  • Ward lighting is bright, cold, and unflattering, and the screens are old and often at an angle
  • Users are standing, interrupted, and frequently wearing gloves
  • Red and amber carry clinical meaning and cannot be spent on anything else

That third constraint was the one that shaped the palette. In most products, a warning colour is a design choice. Here it is a signal with a defined meaning, and using amber for a marketing banner would have been a genuine hazard. So the system has two colour vocabularies — a neutral one for interface, and a clinical one that only the clinical components can reach.

Bigger than it looks

Every target is at least fifty-six pixels, every body size starts at seventeen, and every contrast ratio clears AAA rather than AA. The system looks slightly oversized on a designer's laptop. On a wall-mounted screen at two metres, under a fluorescent tube, it looks correct.

That gap is the lesson I took away. A design system is calibrated to a room, and if you have not been in the room you are calibrating to your own desk.

title: Tiny Atlas
description: A map-making tool for walking routes, with a printer as the only export format.
imageAlt: A hand-drawn walking route inked on a folded topographic sheet
content:
Tiny Atlas makes one thing: a folded paper map of a walk, sized to a single sheet, with an elevation strip along the bottom and nothing else on it.

It has no account system, no sharing, and no app. You draw a route, you press print, and you fold the result into your pocket. The whole project is an argument that some outputs should leave the screen.

Why paper

A phone on a hillside is a battery you are rationing and a screen you cannot read. A paper map is legible in rain, survives being sat on, and does not interrupt the walk to show you a notification. It is also, and this matters more than it should, nice to look at afterwards.

The typography problem

Most of the work went into labels. A map label has to be readable at eight point, in the rain, printed on a domestic inkjet, over a background of contour lines it does not control. The answer turned out to be a heavier weight than looked right on screen, a small halo in the paper colour behind every label, and ruthlessly fewer names than I first wanted.

I have printed about sixty of these. Four are framed.
